one_liner: Eclipse Vert.x's own gRPC server for the JVM; served unary grpc_bench echo 1.75x faster than the gRPC C++ async server in one 2026 run.
what_it_does: A gRPC server (and client) for Java built on the Vert.x HTTP server rather than on grpc-java's Netty transport. A GrpcServer is a Handler<HttpServerRequest>, so it plugs into a Vert.x HttpServer or a Vert.x Web route; services are written either against a request/response stream API (callbacks and Futures) or against stubs generated by the Vert.x gRPC protoc plugin, and in 5.x the grpc-java generated-stub bridge lives in the separate vertx-grpcio-server module. The same server also speaks gRPC-Web, application/grpc+json and HTTP/JSON transcoding by default.
how_it_is_fast: The benchmark gives no mechanism. In the source, GrpcServerImpl handles each gRPC call on the Vert.x context (event loop) that owns the HTTP/2 request, with message framing done on Vert.x Buffers, so there is no hand-off to a separate executor; the grpc_bench app deploys one ServerVerticle per CPU, each with its own HttpServer on its own event loop sharing port 50051. The measurable effect in #559 is CPU per request (derived from page data): about 10.1 us for Vert.x against 18.0 us for cpp_grpc_mt at 1 CPU, and 15.4 us against 47.4 us at 4 CPUs, where the C++ server's per-request CPU rose 2.6x while Vert.x's rose 1.5x.
when_to_use: JVM services that are mostly small unary gRPC calls and need the highest requests per CPU core of the Java options (it topped all 13 JVM rows of grpc_bench #559 at 1 and 4 CPUs).
Applications already on Vert.x or Quarkus, where the gRPC endpoint can share the event loops and the HTTP server with REST routes.
gRPC proxies and gateways: the message-level API forwards protobuf-encoded (even compressed) messages without decoding and re-encoding them.
Services that must expose gRPC-Web or HTTP/JSON transcoding from the same port without an Envoy sidecar.
when_not_to_use: Memory-tight deployments or sidecars: grpc_bench #559 measured 108 to 333 MiB for Vert.x against 21 to 32 MiB for the C++ server and 13 to 15 MiB for Rust tonic.
Tail-latency-bound services: despite lower averages, Vert.x's p99 was worse than C++ in #559 (29.95 ms vs 21.81 ms at 1 CPU, 21.70 ms vs 19.69 ms at 4 CPUs).
Handlers that block (JDBC, file I/O, heavy CPU) unless they are moved off the event loop; a blocking handler stalls every call on that loop.
Short-lived processes or cold-start-sensitive deployments: the measured numbers come after a 30 s JIT warm-up.
Teams that need the C++ result reproduced: three other published grpc_bench runs show only 0.98x to 1.22x over cpp_grpc_mt.

integration.form: module (Maven artifact io.vertx:vertx-grpc-server; vertx-grpcio-server for grpc-java stubs)
integration.dependencies: vertx-core (Vert.x HTTP/2 server on Netty), protobuf-java; protobuf-java-util for the JSON wire format; grpc-java stubs only through vertx-grpcio-server
integration.min_toolchain: Minimum JDK not documented in the pages read; the benchmark built vertx-grpc-server 4.4.4 on eclipse-temurin 23 with Gradle and protoc 3.21.6
integration.platforms: any JVM platform (the benchmark ran on x86-64 Linux in Docker)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented in the gRPC docs; each call is handled on the Vert.x context of its HTTP request (event-loop model), so a handler must not block
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it speaks the standard gRPC over HTTP/2 wire protocol, so existing C++ clients need no change, but the service itself must be rewritten in Java against the Vert.x API

gotchas: Harness flaw in the measured row: java_vertx_grpc_bench/Dockerfile sets ENV JAVA_OPTS (-XX:+UseSerialGC, Min/MaxRAMPercentage=70) but starts the server with an exec-form ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", ...]; the java launcher does not read JAVA_OPTS, so those flags never reached the JVM and Vert.x ran on default JVM ergonomics. The java_hotspot_grpc_* images use the Gradle installDist start script, which does read JAVA_OPTS, so the Vert.x row is not configured like its JVM siblings and the record's compiler_and_flags is wrong on this point.

The 2 to 4 CPU rows look capped outside the server: Vert.x stayed near 150k req/s (148200, 153126, 149776) and used only 230% CPU of a 4-CPU limit, and Quarkus, Armeria, tonic and .NET cluster at 131k to 142k; with a ghz client limited to 11 CPUs and the server reached through a Docker-published port on 127.0.0.1, the 1.88x to 1.99x figures probably measure the C++ server against a shared ceiling. The CPU-bound like-for-like point is 1 CPU (100308 vs 57403 req/s, 1.75x).

The C++ baseline pre-posts a single CallData per completion queue, whereas gRPC's own async QPS benchmark server (test/cpp/qps/server_async.cc) pre-posts 5000 request contexts per queue; it also links an unpinned Debian libgrpc++ build. cpp_asio_grpc lands within about 2% of it, so the ceiling is most likely the packaged gRPC C++ core rather than the app pattern, but the baseline is not gRPC C++ at its tuned best.

Security: the benchmarked vertx-grpc-server 4.4.4 is in the range of CVE-2024-8391 (GHSA-g76f-gjfx-4rpr: no limit on inbound message length, 4.3.0 to 4.5.9, fixed in 4.5.10), and a per-message allocation bound for compressed messages was only added on 2026-10-07 (5.1.9); set a maximum message size and use a current release.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over grpc-dotnet (84809 req/s at 1 CPU), Rust tonic (82515) and Armeria (56315) when the service must stay on the JVM and per-core unary throughput matters most, since it posted 100308 req/s at 1 CPU in the same run; pick tonic instead when memory matters (13 to 15 MiB against 108 to 333 MiB) or p99 latency is the target.
verified_claims_summary: In grpc_bench discussion #559 (maintainer run, commit c4c93b3, Intel Xeon Gold 6548N, ghz 0.114.0 with 50 connections and 1000 concurrent unary complex_proto echo calls, 120 s after a 30 s warm-up), Vert.x gRPC server 4.4.4 on Temurin 23 served 100308 req/s on 1 CPU against 57403 for cpp_grpc_mt (g++ 15.2.0 -O3 -flto glue linked to Debian-packaged libgrpc++ and jemalloc), 1.75x, and 1.75x to 1.99x at 2 to 4 CPUs where the faster rows appear to hit a shared ceiling; earlier published runs (#441, #475, #547) put it only 0.98x to 1.22x ahead.
status_note: Actively maintained Eclipse Vert.x component (5.1.9 released 2026-10-07, 5.3.0-SNAPSHOT on main, dual EPL-2.0/Apache-2.0); the measured 4.4.4 release is old, carries CVE-2024-8391, and its grpc-java MethodDescriptor style of binding moved to vertx-grpcio-server in 5.x, so the benchmark code needs porting before it can be rerun on a current release.
